Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Nazakat Beauty Co.: forty-one lakh customers, or maybe twenty-six

Mumbai, the night of Sunday 22 November 2026. Record festive revenue, falling margin, five channels, five dashboards, and no agreement on what any of the numbers mean.

1. The night before

Ira Malhotra had been at the Nazakat Beauty Co. office in Lower Parel since eleven in the morning, which was unusual for a Sunday and would have been unremarkable to anyone who had seen the board pack. It ran to fifty-one slides. Eleven of them contained numbers that contradicted other numbers in the same pack, and Ira had found seven of the eleven herself that afternoon.

The board met at nine on Monday. Nazakat had just closed its best festive season: ₹86 crore of net revenue in the thirty days spanning Dhanteras and the week after Diwali, against ₹61 crore in the same window in 2025. The chair, who sat on four consumer boards and had a habit of asking one question and then waiting, had circulated his question by email on Friday evening. It had two parts. Which channel is actually growing this business, and who in your company owns the answer?

Ira was Chief Product and Growth Officer. She had joined in 2024 from a larger consumer company and had spent two years discovering that Nazakat's problem was not a shortage of measurement. There were five channel dashboards, a company scorecard, a weekly growth stand-up, a monthly business review and a quarterly board pack. Between them they produced, by her count, 213 distinct numbers a month. What she could not do, on the night of 22 November, was answer either half of the chair's question without three caveats and an argument.

At 9.40 pm Aditya Ravichandran, the company's data scientist, came online from Toronto, where it was mid-morning, and sent her a single line: “I can defend the direction. I cannot defend the size. If they ask for a number I will have to say so.”

2. How Nazakat got here

Nazakat Beauty Co. was founded in 2018 by Tanvi Seth, a former beauty editor, and Raghav Menon, who had run supply chain at a mid-sized FMCG business. It began as a direct-to-consumer colour cosmetics brand built around shade ranges for Indian skin tones, added skincare in 2020, and reached ₹412 crore of net revenue in FY26. It manufactured through three contract facilities in Baddi and Gujarat, held CDSCO registrations for its imported actives, and had a Legal Metrology labelling process that Raghav regarded as the company's least appreciated competitive advantage.

The decision that shaped everything came in January 2022. Nazakat was then selling through its own app and website, through Nykaa, and through Amazon, and the three teams were fighting weekly over inventory and discount depth. The board approved what was called, in the minutes, channel autonomy: each channel would have its own leader, its own P&L, its own targets and its own dashboard. It worked. Revenue tripled in three years and the fighting largely stopped.

The same board meeting approved a three-year contract with a customer-data platform vendor, Solvei, to unify customer records. Solvei's identity graph keyed on email address and mobile number. That was adequate in 2022, when 78 per cent of revenue came from channels where Nazakat saw both. The contract was renewed in 2025 through March 2028 at ₹2.4 crore a year, with an exit penalty of ₹1.8 crore, three months before quick commerce became Nazakat's second-largest channel — a channel in which Nazakat sees neither an email address nor a phone number, ever.

Those two decisions, taken in the same room on the same morning, are why Ira's board pack contains eleven contradictions. Channel autonomy created five owners of five different customer counts. The Solvei architecture made it structurally impossible to reconcile them.

3. The industry around it

By late 2026 Indian beauty retail had reorganised itself around three forces. Nykaa remained the category's centre of gravity for discovery and had built a substantial physical footprint; Reliance Retail's Tira and a dense field of marketplace sellers had compressed marketplace economics; and quick commerce had done something nobody in the category had modelled in 2022, which was to make a ₹399 lipstick a ten-minute impulse purchase. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart together now moved a meaningful share of mass colour cosmetics, and their terms — margin, listing fees, ad spend, fill-rate penalties — were negotiated afresh each quarter.

Regulation shaped the data problem directly. The DPDP Act's consent architecture meant that joining a quick-commerce buyer to a Nazakat D2C identity required notice and consent Nazakat had no mechanism to collect, since it never met that buyer. The quick-commerce contracts themselves prohibited the sharing of customer-level personal data, and Nazakat's counsel had advised in June 2026 that even probabilistic matching on delivery pin code and basket signature sat in territory the company should not enter before the rules on consent managers settled. ONDC had opened an alternative path that two of Nazakat's competitors were testing and that Raghav considered unproven.

Abroad, Nazakat sold into the GCC through Suhail Trading LLC, a Dubai distributor with a 2,100-outlet reach across the UAE and Oman, and ran a US Amazon storefront managed by Harish Iyer from New Jersey, mostly serving the diaspora. Together the two contributed ₹5.2 crore in the festive month at the best contribution margin in the business — and the least reliable data, since distributor sell-out was an estimate that arrived quarterly.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In August 2025, after a planning offsite, Nazakat adopted a North Star metric: monthly active customers. The intention was to stop the channel leaders arguing about GMV and get them arguing about customers. Each channel lead was asked to report their monthly active customers into the company scorecard. Each did. Nobody wrote down a single definition, and by the time anyone noticed, five definitions were in production. Exhibit 2 shows them.

Through 2026 the scorecard number rose steadily and pleasingly, from 28 lakh in January to 41 lakh in the festive month. It was quoted in the Series B extension memo in March and in two press interviews. In September, preparing for the Series C conversation, Aditya ran a matched-panel analysis on the 62,000 Nazakat Circle members who had linked a quick-commerce order to their loyalty ID. It suggested that between 22 and 31 per cent of quick-commerce buyers in that panel had also bought on D2C in the same month. Applied crudely to the whole base, that implied the true unique customer count was somewhere between 26 and 31 lakh, not 41. The panel was self-selected, so the estimate was soft in a direction Aditya could not sign.

In October, Aditya ran something more ambitious: a geographic holdout across fourteen pin-code clusters, halving quick-commerce trade spend in six of them for nine weeks. The headline result was that 62 per cent of quick-commerce GMV in the test clusters was incremental, implying 38 per cent substitution from other channels, principally D2C. The confidence interval ran from 48 to 76 per cent. Then Zepto expanded into three of the six control clusters in week five, and two test clusters ran out of the hero SKU during Dhanteras. Aditya's note to Ira said the study was directionally usable and quantitatively compromised, which is the most honest and least useful thing a data scientist can say a week before a board meeting.

The third thing that turned out to be wrong arrived on 18 November, when Pallavi Deshmukh closed the festive month. Blended contribution margin after COGS, platform fees, fulfilment and channel marketing — what Nazakat called CM2 — had fallen to 17.7 per cent from 24.1 per cent in the same window a year earlier, on revenue up 41 per cent. Pallavi's bridge allocated all brand marketing across channels in proportion to revenue. Ira's growth team maintained a parallel bridge that treated brand marketing as a company-level investment and did not allocate it, which produced 21.0 per cent. Both had been circulated. Both were in the board pack. Nobody had ever decided which one was the company's number, because no one owned the definition.

5. The people

Tanvi Seth, co-founder and CEO, Mumbai. Position: the D2C app is the brand's home and the only place Nazakat owns the customer; she wants the board pack to lead with D2C and Circle enrolment. Incentive: her equity outcome depends on the Series C multiple. Not saying: an investor told her in October that D2C revenue share is the single input that moves the multiple most, and she has not shared that conversation with Ira.

Raghav Menon, co-founder and COO, Mumbai. Position: channel autonomy works, the P&Ls are clean, and the answer to a measurement problem is not a reorganisation. Incentive: his operating bonus is tied to gross margin and fill rate. Not saying: quick-commerce fill rate in the festive month was 88.4 per cent against a contractual 95, which cost ₹41 lakh in penalties and an unknown amount in lost baskets, and the miss was a planning error in his own team.

Kabir Dhillon, Head of Quick Commerce, Gurugram. Position: quick commerce is the growth engine and should take the largest share of the ₹14 crore Q4 trade budget. Incentive: his variable pay is 70 per cent on quick-commerce GMV growth. Not saying: he has read Aditya's substitution estimate, believes the 38 per cent figure is roughly right, and has not raised it in any forum.

Sneha Bhosale, Head of D2C, Mumbai. Position: D2C repeat rate has improved from 31 to 38 per cent and proves the brand is building equity. Incentive: her targets are app MAU and repeat rate. Not saying: she suspects much of the repeat-rate gain is compositional — low-value first-time buyers have migrated to quick commerce, leaving a higher-intent cohort behind — and has asked Aditya twice, informally, not to put that in writing before the board meeting.

Devika Nambiar, Head of Retail and Marketplace, Bengaluru. Position: Nykaa and the physical counters do the discovery that quick commerce then harvests, and the attribution model gives her none of the credit. Incentive: her channel's revenue target. Not saying: counter-level sell-out is keyed manually by promoters and arrives six weeks late, so her discovery claim is not currently testable with her own data.

Pallavi Deshmukh, CFO, Mumbai. Position: CM2 is the only number that matters and it is falling. Incentive: a clean Series C process. Not saying: her allocation of brand marketing by revenue share was a convention adopted in 2023 for a lender covenant, never revisited, and she is aware it now flatters no one and penalises D2C.

Aditya Ravichandran, Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: no cross-channel customer metric Nazakat currently reports is defensible, and the company should stop reporting them. Incentive: his contract ends in March 2027 and he would like it renewed. Not saying: his holdout study's control contamination is severe enough that a rigorous reviewer might discard the point estimate entirely.

Charmaine Yeo, Regional Operations Lead, Singapore. Position: the GCC business is the most profitable line in the company and deserves investment. Incentive: regional revenue. Not saying: she has seen Nazakat SKUs in two Sharjah outlets that Suhail Trading's territory list does not cover, and suspects a share of the Dubai growth is parallel trade rather than demand.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Every channel is growing and the blended margin is down six points. That is arithmetically possible and commercially alarming. Somebody in this company should be able to tell me which of those two sentences is the important one.”

— the chair, email to Tanvi Seth and Ira Malhotra, Friday 20 November, 7.14 pm

“I'm not going to defend 41 lakh in front of a Series C diligence team. If you want a customer number in the deck, it has to be D2C plus Circle-linked quick commerce, and that number is 8.1 lakh. It is small and it is true.”

— Aditya Ravichandran, Toronto, in the growth channel, Thursday 19 November

“With respect, Aditya has never sat in a Blinkit quarterly review. They gave us 46 per cent of the trade plan because we grew 118 per cent. If we cut that to fund an identity project, we lose the shelf and we don't get it back. The shelf is the asset.”

— Kabir Dhillon, Gurugram, reply in the same thread, four minutes later

“Repeat rate up seven points in a year is the single best thing that has happened to this brand. I would ask everyone to be careful about explaining it away before we've actually measured the explanation.”

— Sneha Bhosale, Mumbai, monthly business review, 12 November

“My promoters at the Shoppers Stop counters in Pune have people walking in, matching a shade on the tester, photographing the code and ordering it on Zepto in the queue. I can show you fourteen videos. I cannot show you a number, because the only number I have arrives six weeks late and is typed by the same promoter.”

— Devika Nambiar, Bengaluru, monthly business review, 12 November

“Can I ask a design question that is really a metric question? The shade finder is measured on sessions. Nobody measures whether it reduces returns. Returns are the thing customers actually experience. Who owns returns?”

— Jonas Ehrlich, Principal Designer, Berlin, product review, 6 November

“Please don't allocate brand spend by revenue in the board pack. It makes D2C look expensive and quick commerce look efficient, and that is an artefact of a covenant we satisfied two years ago.”

— Ira Malhotra to Pallavi Deshmukh, 19 November. Pallavi's reply: “Then someone needs to approve a new basis. Who?”

8. The options as Ira sees them

By Sunday evening Ira had written three options on the whiteboard in the small meeting room, and she was uneasy about all of them in a way she had not yet been able to articulate.

Option one: unify identity and appoint one owner. Exit or renegotiate Solvei, build an identity layer that can accept partial signals, put a single named owner on a single cross-channel customer metric. The exit penalty is ₹1.8 crore and the build is at least nine months. The deeper difficulty is not cost: it is that Exhibit 6 and the DPDP position suggest the ceiling on cross-channel identity is a matter of law and contract, not engineering. Ira has written “can we even get to 60%?” next to this option, twice.

Option two: keep channel autonomy, impose common definitions, add a convening owner. Leave the P&Ls alone; ratify one definition of each contested metric; create a monthly cross-channel review that Ira convenes, with Aditya as definitional steward, and measure incrementality at geography and cohort level rather than person level, since that is what the data will actually support. Cheap, fast, and possibly too small a response to a six-point margin decline.

Option three: collapse the channels into one P&L. Make Ira accountable for a single contribution-margin-based North Star, reduce the channel leads to execution, and end the incentive structure that makes Kabir's bonus point away from the company's margin. Decisive, and it undoes the one structural decision that everyone agrees produced three years of growth. Raghav has said privately that Kabir would leave within a quarter, and that the Blinkit relationship is Kabir's, not Nazakat's.

What Ira had not resolved, and what kept her at the office, was a suspicion that all three options answered the second half of the chair's question and none of them answered the first. Every option was a proposal about who owns a metric. None of them said which decision the metric was for. And there was a live decision, with a date on it: ₹14 crore of Q4 trade spend, 46 per cent of it currently pointed at the channel with a 9.4 per cent contribution margin and an incrementality estimate whose interval spanned two opposite conclusions.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday 23 November. The Series C term sheet is indicative and expires on 15 December; diligence would begin in the first week of January. The ₹14 crore Q4 trade commitment must be signed with the three quick-commerce partners and the two marketplaces by 30 November, and the quick-commerce terms are annual-volume-linked, so a cut now reprices the whole of 2027. The Solvei contract runs to March 2028 with an ₹1.8 crore exit penalty. There is a hiring freeze above ₹35 lakh CTC until the round closes; Aditya's Toronto contract expires in March 2027 and renewing it at market would breach that threshold. Counsel's June advice on probabilistic matching stands and has not been revisited. Suhail Trading's next order, ₹3.1 crore, is due for confirmation on 28 November, and Charmaine has asked for a week to check something she has not fully explained.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct the chain of decisions from January 2022 to November 2026 that produced Exhibit 2. At which point, with what was known then, could someone have prevented it — and what would they have had to give up?

2. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 4 describe the same month. What decision would you take differently depending on which of the two you believed, and who in this company has the standing to ratify one of them?

3. Exhibit 3 is the only direct evidence on the chair's first question, and it is compromised. Is a contaminated study with a wide interval better or worse than no study, given that a ₹14 crore commitment must be signed in eight days? What would you do with it in the board meeting?

4. Take any three rows of Exhibit 5 and write the owner, cadence, trigger and decision you would assign. For which rows does the exercise turn out to be impossible, and what does the impossibility tell you?

5. Sneha, Kabir, Devika and Pallavi each hold a position that is defensible from where they sit and that also serves their compensation. Is Nazakat's problem a measurement problem, an incentive problem, or a structural one — and can it be diagnosed without first fixing the measurement?

6. What should Ira do on Monday morning, in what order, and what exactly should she say to the chair when he asks his two questions? Which of the eleven contradictions in the board pack should she surface herself, and which should she leave alone?

11. 11.40 pm

Ira turned off the projector and looked at the whiteboard. Three options, and next to them, in a different colour, a list she had started at eight o'clock and not shown anyone: the seven contradictions she had found, the four she suspected were there and had not found, and a single line at the bottom that read what is the decision we are trying to make.

Her phone showed a message from Charmaine in Singapore, sent at 1.10 am her time: “Can we speak before the board? Not about the metrics. About Sharjah.” Below it, unread, a message from Tanvi: “Let's lead with D2C and Circle. Keep it simple for them.” And below that, from Aditya in Toronto, who had gone offline an hour ago and come back: “One more thing. I pulled the repeat-rate cohorts by first-order value. Sneha is going to want to see this before tomorrow. Do you want me to send it to her, or to you?”

The board met in nine and a half hours. Ira had not yet answered any of the three.
exp20v2-met.metric.ownership:
Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Metric Ownership and Cadence

Who owns this metric, and what decision does it change?

1. A dashboard with forty-two metrics and no one in charge

On the morning of 18 September 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Charvi Foods, a Bengaluru quick-commerce grocery app promising forty-five-minute delivery, sat through her third consecutive weekly metrics review that ended without a decision. The dashboard projected onto the wall carried forty-two tiles: weekly active users, cart abandonment, dark-store stock availability, rider acceptance rate, net promoter score, average basket value, and thirty-six others accumulated over eighteen months as different teams asked analytics to "just add one more chart." Weekly active users had been flat at 3.1 million for nine weeks. Everyone in the room had a theory. No one owned the number.

The stakes were concrete. Charvi had closed a ₹210 crore Series B in March, and the board wanted a credible growth plan before authorising a Pune launch budgeted at ₹18 crore for the December quarter. Karthik Iyer, who ran supply chain from Pune, blamed stock-outs. Farhan Sheikh, operations lead in Chennai, blamed rider shortages during evening peak. Meher Chopra, the Hyderabad-based analytics lead, pointed out that six of the forty-two metrics had not moved a single review's decision in the past two months — they were reported because someone once asked for them, not because anyone acted on them. Ananya's problem was not a shortage of data. It was that no metric had a name and a date attached to it: an owner accountable for its value, and a cadence at which that owner was required to look at it and decide something.

2. The idea: a name and a date next to every number

Metric ownership and cadence is the discipline of attaching three things to every number a company tracks: a single accountable owner, a review rhythm matched to how quickly the underlying reality changes, and an explicit statement of the decision the metric exists to inform. A metric with no owner is read by everyone and acted on by no one; a metric with no cadence is either checked so rarely that it cannot catch problems in time, or checked so often that noise is mistaken for signal; a metric with no attached decision survives on a dashboard indefinitely because nobody can say what would happen if it disappeared.

The practice has two lineages that merged over the 2010s. One is the Objectives and Key Results discipline that Andy Grove built at Intel and John Doerr later popularised in Silicon Valley, which insisted that a key result without a named owner was not a commitment, only a wish. The other is the growth-team tradition — visible in how Facebook's growth organisation and later the Reforge curriculum taught metric trees — which decomposed a single North Star metric into driver metrics, each assigned to the function that could actually move it. Metric ownership and cadence is what happens when you take the accountability habit from the first tradition and apply it to every node of the tree from the second. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: every metric on our dashboard should have someone's name next to it and a date on the calendar when they are required to act on it, or it should not be on the dashboard.

Figure 1. A three-level metric tree for Charvi's fulfilment rate, with an owner and a cadence assigned at every node — not just at the top.

3. How the assignment actually gets done

The mechanics are less about statistics than about organisational discipline, and practitioners routinely skip the first step because it feels like busywork. First, build the metric tree: decompose the North Star metric — the single number the team agrees best represents value delivered, in Charvi's case the 45-minute fulfilment rate — into the driver metrics that multiply or add up to it. Second, and this is the step most teams skip, assign exactly one accountable owner to each node, not a committee. A RACI chart with three "responsible" names for one metric is a sign that nobody is actually accountable; the owner is the person who loses a Friday afternoon explaining the number if it moves the wrong way, not the analyst who computes it. Third, set the cadence by asking how quickly the underlying reality can change and how expensive a delayed reaction would be — not by defaulting every metric to the company's existing weekly all-hands rhythm. Fourth, write down, in one sentence, the decision the metric informs: what specifically changes if the number crosses a threshold. Fifth, set a retirement trigger in advance — a metric that has not changed a decision in two review cycles is a candidate for removal, decided at the moment of creation rather than argued about later when someone is attached to their chart.

MetricOwnerCadenceDecision it informs
45-minute fulfilment rateAnanya RaoWeekly, board monthlyWhether to fund driver-level fixes or hold spend
Stock availabilityKarthik IyerDailyTrigger emergency replenishment below 85%
Rider acceptance rateFarhan SheikhDaily, hourly in surgeOpen surge incentives or add rider shifts
Weekly active usersUnowned before SeptemberWeekly, no thresholdNone — retired after the review

Table 1. Charvi's revised metric register. Note the fourth row: a widely watched number with no owner, no threshold and no decision attached — exactly the profile that marks a metric for retirement.

4. Charvi's arithmetic, worked through

Ananya's team modelled the fulfilment rate as the product of three driver metrics for the week ending 13 September 2026: stock availability at 92%, rider acceptance rate at 88%, and on-time completion given a rider accepted the order at 95%. Multiplying these gives 0.92 × 0.88 × 0.95 = 0.7697, a 45-minute fulfilment rate of 76.97%. Each of the three inputs already had a named owner in the tree above, but only stock availability had ever been discussed in a weekly review; the other two were buried in an operations dashboard nobody outside Chennai opened.

Karthik proposed a ₹40 lakh investment in predictive replenishment for the Bengaluru dark stores, projected to lift stock availability from 92% to 96% within six weeks, with rider acceptance and on-time completion held constant. Recomputing: 0.96 × 0.88 × 0.95 = 0.8026, or 80.26% — a gain of 3.29 percentage points on the North Star. At Charvi's roughly 62,000 daily orders, a 3.29-point improvement in fulfilment translates to about 2,040 additional successfully completed orders per day, which the finance team valued at close to ₹9 lakh in daily contribution margin, comfortably justifying the ₹40 lakh spend within a week. The second pass mattered because it showed the board a number tied to a named lever and a named owner, rather than a flat statement that "fulfilment is improving." That is the entire discipline in miniature: an owner, a cadence at which Karthik reports stock availability, and a decision — fund or defer the replenishment system — that the metric alone answered.

5. The distinctions a learner must hold onto

Owner is not the same as analyst

The person who builds the dashboard query is rarely the person who should own the metric. Ownership means the authority and obligation to act on the number, which usually sits with a function head, not with whoever in analytics happens to have write access to the SQL.

Cadence follows decision latency, not habit

A metric should be reviewed as often as the decision it informs can actually be changed, and no more often. Reviewing rider acceptance daily makes sense because staffing can be adjusted daily; reviewing customer lifetime value daily is theatre, since nothing meaningful moves that fast.

A decision-linked metric differs from a vanity metric

Weekly active users looked reassuring on Charvi's dashboard for months precisely because it moved slowly and comfortably; it was not attached to any single decision, which is why nobody could say what a 2% drop would require them to do.

Multiplicative trees hide correlation as causation

Stock availability, rider acceptance and on-time completion are not independent; a stock-out can itself trigger longer rider wait times, which depresses acceptance. Ownership assigns accountability per node, but a thoughtful owner still asks whether moving their number will move a neighbour's for reasons the tree does not show.

Reorganisation is the silent killer of ownership

When Charvi merged its ops and supply-chain functions in 2025, three metrics quietly lost their owner for two quarters because nobody re-assigned them during the transition; ownership must be reconfirmed at every org change, not assumed to survive it.

Ownership cannot fix bad instrumentation

Naming Karthik the owner of stock availability does nothing if the underlying inventory feed from Charvi's dark stores updates only twice a day; ownership assigns accountability for acting on a number, not for the number being trustworthy in the first place.

A dashboard is not a governance system

Publishing a metric widely is often mistaken for having assigned it an owner. Visibility and accountability are different axes entirely, and the newcomer's first question in any review should be: if this number moved sharply next week, whose job would change because of it?

6. How this differs by product type and by stage

In a consumer product like Charvi, driver metrics tend to be operational and fast-moving — stock, riders, delivery windows — so cadences cluster around daily and weekly. In a B2B product, the equivalent tree often runs through account health and renewal signals that move on a quarterly or even annual clock, so a metric owner in enterprise software is more often a customer-success lead reviewing monthly, not daily. Marketplace products complicate ownership further because a single metric, such as a match rate between buyers and sellers, sits on both sides of the business simultaneously; Charvi's own rider-acceptance metric has this flavour, since it depends on both demand density and rider supply, which is why Ananya ultimately gave joint accountability to Farhan for supply-side actions and to the city-launch team for demand-side ones, rather than pretending one owner could move both levers.

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage team can tolerate loose ownership because the founder personally tracks everything; the discipline becomes non-negotiable once a company crosses roughly fifty people, the point at which Charvi found itself in 2026, because no single person can hold forty-two metrics in their head anymore, and the review meeting becomes the only place accountability is visible at all.

7. Where teams go wrong

Ownership assigned to whoever built the chart

Symptom: the metric is discussed but nobody in the room can authorise a change. Underlying error: mistaking data production for decision authority. Cheapest diagnostic: ask who would be paged if the number moved 10% overnight — if the answer is "the analytics team," ownership is misassigned.

One cadence for every metric

Symptom: weekly reviews that spend equal time on numbers that barely move and numbers that need daily attention. Underlying error: copying the company's meeting rhythm onto every metric instead of matching cadence to decision speed. Cheapest diagnostic: for each metric, ask how many times in the last quarter the review actually changed a plan.

Dashboard bloat from never retiring metrics

Symptom: forty-two tiles, as at Charvi, six of which nobody has acted on in two months. Underlying error: treating metric creation as free and metric removal as politically costly. Cheapest diagnostic: for each metric, name the last decision it changed; if no one can, retire it.

8. What good looks like

Six months after the September review, Charvi's dashboard carried nineteen metrics, not forty-two. Every tile listed a name, a cadence, and one sentence describing the decision it served — Karthik's stock-availability tile, reviewed daily, read "triggers emergency replenishment order below 85%." When rider acceptance dipped in Hyderabad during Diwali week, Farhan did not wait for the weekly review; his cadence for that metric was already daily during festival surge periods, a cadence he had set himself because he, not analytics, owned the consequence of missing it. The board no longer heard forty-two numbers; it heard the six that mattered, each with a name attached, and each one traceable to a decision that had actually been made because of it.

9. What Ananya decided, and two questions

Ananya rebuilt Charvi's metric tree around the fulfilment rate, assigned single owners to every node, matched cadence to how fast each driver could realistically move, and set a standing rule that any metric surviving two review cycles without changing a decision would be retired. She approved Karthik's ₹40 lakh replenishment investment on the strength of the recomputed 80.26% projection, and moved rider-acceptance review to daily during demand surges at Farhan's own request. The next topic worth her attention is metric trees and driver models themselves — the discipline of decomposing a North Star correctly in the first place, since ownership only works once the tree it hangs on is built well.

Two questions worth sitting with: for the metric your own team checks most often, who would actually lose an afternoon if it moved the wrong way — and can you name the decision it last changed, or only the meeting it was discussed in?
case20v1-met.metric.ownership:
Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Nirvaha Payroll: thirty-two metrics and one blind spot

Bengaluru, March 2026. A company that measures everything discovers it has been losing its most valuable customers for four months without noticing.

1. Thursday, 5 March 2026

The Growth & Health Review at Nirvaha Payroll ran every Thursday at four in the afternoon in a glass room on the fourth floor of an office block in Koramangala, Bengaluru. It had thirty-two metrics, a fixed running order, and a habit of finishing on time. On 5 March it did not finish on time, because Wei Ling Tan had dialled in from Singapore with a slide the data team had not prepared.

Wei Ling ran customer success for Nirvaha's accounts outside India. Her slide listed eleven customers in the 200-to-500 employee band who had either given notice or asked for a contract review since November. Nine of the eleven had cited the same two things: a payroll run that had slipped past their internal cut-off during the Diwali fortnight, and a delay in the EPFO challan generation that had forced their HR teams to file manually.

Meera Iyengar, Nirvaha's VP Product, looked at the dashboard behind Wei Ling's slide. Blended monthly logo churn, the number the room had watched for two years, read 1.6 per cent. In September it had read 1.5 per cent. By the metric the company reviewed every week, nothing had happened at all. Meera had eight days. The Series B partner meeting was on 24 March, and the board had asked her for a metrics pack and an operating-model proposal by Friday 13 March.

2. Nirvaha Payroll

Nirvaha was founded in 2019 by Anand Bhattacharya and Meera Iyengar to do one unglamorous thing well: run payroll for Indian companies with twenty to five hundred employees and keep them compliant. The product calculated salaries, deducted TDS and professional tax, generated EPFO and ESIC challans, filed returns, and pushed an employee app that showed payslips, Form 16 and leave balances. Payouts moved over bank APIs and UPI; the company held a data-processor obligation under the DPDP Act, which mattered greatly to its larger customers' legal teams.

By March 2026 Nirvaha had 7,400 paying companies, processed 6.1 lakh employee records a month, and carried ₹58 crore of ARR. It sat in a crowded market: Zoho Payroll and greytHR below it on price, Keka and RazorpayX Payroll alongside, Darwinbox above it in the enterprise tier. Its differentiation had always been statutory reliability — the claim that a Nirvaha customer never missed a filing deadline.

The team was spread across time zones by accident rather than design. Vikrant Deshpande's platform engineering group sat in Pune. Lena Brückner, the principal designer, worked from Berlin. Aparna Raghunathan, the data scientist who had built most of the dashboard, had moved to Toronto in 2024 and stayed. Wei Ling covered Singapore, Dubai and the ASEAN accounts, including Nahda Retail Group, a 2,100-employee distributor in Dubai that had signed in 2025 and needed UAE Wage Protection System files alongside its Indian payroll. Douglas Fernandes sold from New Jersey to Indian-founded companies with US subsidiaries.

3. The situation

Meera spent Friday and the weekend reconstructing what had been knowable and when. Aparna pulled the churn series segmented by employee band — a cut that existed in the warehouse but had never been on the dashboard, because the dashboard had been built in 2023 when 92 per cent of Nirvaha's customers were under fifty employees.

The picture that came back is Exhibit 2. Blended logo churn had been flat at 1.5 to 1.6 per cent for six months, because it was dominated by the micro band, where a stable trickle of small companies had always come and gone. Underneath it, monthly ARR churn had risen from 0.9 per cent to 2.1 per cent, and almost all of the rise came from the 200-to-500 band, where Nirvaha earned an average of ₹4.9 lakh per customer per year against ₹22,900 in the micro band. The company had been watching a count and living off a value.

Meera then audited the review itself, metric by metric, which produced Exhibit 1. Of thirty-two metrics, nine had a named individual who would be asked to explain a movement; five had a written threshold at which anything would happen; two had changed a decision in the previous quarter. Two of the metrics most directly implicated in the eleven departures — payroll-run success rate and statutory filing on-time rate — were not on the dashboard at all. They existed on Vikrant's engineering monitoring, reviewed by his on-call rota and by nobody else, and during the Diwali fortnight the on-time filing rate had fallen to 96.1 per cent from a usual 99.4 per cent for eleven consecutive working days.

Vikrant's position, put bluntly in the Monday follow-up, was that this was not a measurement failure at all but a capacity failure, and that adding metrics would not add servers. Aparna's position from Toronto, sent as a long message at two in the morning Bengaluru time, was that Nirvaha had eleven different definitions of “active customer” in circulation and that no amount of ownership would help until somebody was accountable for definitions. Anand wanted something simpler: one number for the Series B deck and a story about discipline.

4. The people

Meera Iyengar, VP Product, Bengaluru. Accountable for the proposal due on 13 March. Believes the company's instinct will be to add metrics and that this would be the wrong lesson.

Anand Bhattacharya, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Wants the metrics pack to be clean and short, and is nervous that a segmented churn exhibit will read to investors as an admission. Has said he will support “whatever is rigorous”, which Meera reads as genuine but conditional.

Wei Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Has the earliest and best information in the company and no metric of her own, no standing agenda slot, and a 2.5-hour offset that puts her at the end of every Indian working day. Wants a named renewal-risk metric she can own, and the authority to trigger a response without routing through Bengaluru.

Vikrant Deshpande, Engineering Director, Pune. Owns payroll-run success and filing on-time rate on his monitoring stack, with alarm thresholds and a paging rota. Resists their promotion to a business dashboard, reasonably: he fears a weekly forum second-guessing operational judgement, and he points out that the November incident was detected and resolved within hours — what failed was that nobody connected it to renewals.

Aparna Raghunathan, Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants a central metrics function that owns definitions and certifies a single source of truth. Has argued for this twice before and been told it was premature.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Audit of the Thursday review, 32 metrics, conducted 6–8 March 2026.

Exhibit 2. Customers, ARR and churn by employee band, September 2025 and February 2026.

Churn rates are monthly. ARR churn is gross, excluding expansion. February ARR churn of 2.1 per cent represents ₹1.22 crore of annualised revenue lost in one month, of which ₹0.79 crore came from the 200–500 band. Aparna's note flags that the 200–500 band has only 450 customers, so a single month's rate carries a wide band of uncertainty; the three-month trend does not.

6. The options

Option A: charter every surviving metric and tier the cadence. Give each metric that survives an audit a named individual owner, a derived review cadence and a written trigger; retire the rest to a queryable archive. Split the Thursday meeting into a 30-minute weekly operating review of eight metrics, a monthly business review of twelve metrics always presented segmented by band, and an alarm channel carrying Vikrant's thresholds. Give Wei Ling ownership of a renewal-risk metric with a standing slot. The upside is that it addresses the actual failure — no segmentation, no owner, no trigger — without adding headcount. The cost is roughly six weeks of Meera's and Aparna's time, a political fight over retirement, and no new capability if the underlying platform problem recurs.

Option B: build a central metrics function. Hire three analysts under Aparna in Toronto to own definitions, certify a single dashboard and serve the business teams, at about ₹1.1 crore a year. The upside is that it fixes the eleven-definitions problem permanently and gives Nirvaha a data capability it will need at ₹150 crore of ARR. The cost is money at an awkward moment, a nine-and-a-half-hour offset between the certifiers and the decision-makers, and the risk that the data team becomes the nominal owner of every metric — owning numbers it cannot move.

Option C: collapse to a North Star and quarterly OKRs. Retire the weekly review entirely; adopt net revenue retention as the single company metric; run quarterly OKRs beneath it. The upside is radical simplicity and a clean story for the Series B. The cost is that a quarterly cadence would have caught the 200-to-500 band problem in April rather than March, and net revenue retention at Nirvaha's scale moves on a twelve-month lag — the company would be steering by a number that reports the past year.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 2 and Figure 2 contain the same underlying data as the dashboard the team watched every week. Why did the weekly review fail to surface the problem, and which of the three failures — wrong metric, wrong cut, wrong cadence, or no owner — was doing the most damage?

2. Vikrant already owned the filing on-time rate, with a threshold and a paging rota, and the November incident was resolved in hours. In what sense, then, was that metric unowned?

3. Wei Ling had the earliest information in the company. What would it take, concretely, to convert her judgement into something reviewable — and what would be lost in the conversion?

4. Which option should Meera propose on 13 March, and what exactly should the Series B metrics pack show about the last six months?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about a company that measured a great deal and owned almost none of it. The lens is the three-part test: every metric needs an owner who can act, a cadence derived from how fast the metric moves and how fast the team can respond, and a decision it would change at a stated threshold. Apply the test to Nirvaha's thirty-two metrics and twenty-three fail it outright.

Notice that the blind spot was not caused by measuring too little. All the data existed. It was caused by three specific gaps. The dashboard carried a count metric (logo churn) as the proxy for a value problem, and the two diverge whenever customer value is unevenly distributed — at Nirvaha, 450 customers out of 7,400 carried 38 per cent of the revenue. The one cut that would have exposed it, segmentation by band, had no owner and therefore never appeared. And the operational metric that caused the damage was owned in the engineering sense — alarm, threshold, rota — but had no owner in the business sense, so nobody was accountable for asking what an eleven-day filing lapse would do to renewals ninety days later.

A defensible path is Option A, with one element of Option B folded in and Option C rejected on cadence grounds. Meera proposes the charter-and-tier model, and inside it makes Aparna the steward of definitions — accountable for the canonical meaning of “active customer”, “churn” and “ARR” and for reconciling them with finance — without making her the owner of any business metric, since she cannot move one from Toronto. Wei Ling becomes owner of renewal risk in the 50-plus bands, reviewed monthly with a trigger at three at-risk accounts in a rolling thirty days. Vikrant keeps his alarms unchanged and additionally co-owns a single business-facing metric, statutory filing on-time rate, reviewed monthly against a 99 per cent floor, on the explicit argument that it is a leading indicator of value churn with a ninety-day lag. Churn is reviewed monthly, always segmented, never blended.

Option C is the tempting answer and the wrong one, for a reason worth remembering: simplifying the metric set is correct, but a single lagging metric on a quarterly cadence is simplification in the wrong dimension. The cure for thirty-two unowned metrics is not one unowned metric. As for the Series B pack, the strongest version shows the segmented exhibit, names the cause, and states the operating change — because an investor who finds the same cut in diligence will reach a much worse conclusion about the team than one who is handed it.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Metric Ownership and Cadence

Who owns this metric, what decision does it change, and how often does that decision actually get made?

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On Tuesday 4 August 2026, in a glass room in Lower Parel, Ira Bhattacharya, Chief Product Officer of Vindhya Credit Exchange, was asked a question she could not answer honestly. Vindhya is a digital lending marketplace: borrowers apply through its app, and nine partner NBFCs and two banks underwrite against their own board-approved credit policies, roughly 4,000 applications a working day. The headline metric on the operating review, present since the Series B, is the blended approval rate. It had fallen from 62.4% in June to 58.1% in the last week of July, and the investor on the call wanted to know what product was doing about it.

Ira had owned the metric for two years, and could not move it. Approval is decided by partner credit policies she does not write, on an applicant mix set by a marketing budget she does not control, routed by an allocation engine her partnerships counterpart, Nachiket Bose in Delhi, tunes weekly against commercial terms. Zoya Kachwala, who runs analytics from Kolkata, had a slide showing that each of the eleven partners had raised its own approval rate that quarter. Nobody drew the obvious conclusion, because the metric had an owner and therefore appeared to be governed.

Eleven days later, on Saturday 15 August, Girish Pai stood on a shop floor in Chakan, outside Pune, holding a controller board with a swollen capacitor. Girish is VP Product at Shrenik Systems, which sells connected energy- and machine-monitoring controllers to mid-sized manufacturers — 26,000 units live across 340 plants, shipping some 620 a week, with a subscription analytics layer on top. Shrenik's quality metric of record is the 30-day post-install fault rate, reviewed monthly, owned jointly by Girish and Lalitha Krishnan, who runs field engineering from Coimbatore. The capacitor came from a batch that entered production in the second week of June, and the metric had not moved. It could not have. Units ship, sit in a customer's stores, get installed three to five weeks later, accrue a thirty-day fault window, and surface through weekly ticket batches: eleven weeks between a change on the line and a change in the number. By then 7,400 units had shipped.

Ira's problem and Girish's look like opposites — an owner without levers, and a lever without a timely signal — but they are one problem seen from two sides, and the discipline that resolves both is the one most companies believe they already practise.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Metric ownership and cadence is the practice of binding four things to every number a company governs: a definition owner, the only person who may change what it means; a decision owner, one named individual accountable for acting on it; a review cadence, the interval at which that person must look and decide; and a pre-committed decision rule, written before the number is known, stating what will be done at which threshold. A metric missing any one of the four is not governed. It is merely displayed.

Three lineages were stitched together late and imperfectly. The oldest is statistical process control: Shewhart's control charts of the 1920s and Deming's insistence that most variation is common-cause, belongs to the system rather than any person, and that reacting to it makes the process worse. From this comes the quantitative theory of cadence — review a number at the frequency at which it can tell you something, not the frequency at which you meet. The second is management by objectives as Andrew Grove rebuilt it at Intel: output measures, each with a name attached, and his rule of paired indicators, every quantity measure shadowed by a quality measure, because a single owned number invites its own corruption. The third is the growth-team tradition of the 2010s, which decomposed a north-star metric into a tree of drivers, each node given to the function that could move it.

Four positions on this material are genuinely held, and are not reconcilable by good will.

The single-threaded owner school holds that accountability cannot be divided; two owners are zero owners. It will sign that every metric in a review resolves to exactly one name, and that shared ownership of an interface metric is the commonest cause of drift. It will not sign that the owner must control the metric; it accepts accountability for a number one can only influence, and treats the discomfort as productive.

The systems school, descended from Deming, holds the opposite. It will sign that a metric belongs to a process and that cadence derives from the process's control limits. It will not sign putting an individual's name against a number driven mostly by system variation, which produces fear, gaming and tampering rather than improvement.

The pre-committed rule school, whose clearest modern statement is the site-reliability error budget, holds that the decisive artefact is not the person but the if-then. It will sign that a metric without a written threshold and consequence is decorative. It will not sign that judgement at review time suffices, because review time is where thresholds get renegotiated.

The anti-target school takes Goodhart's law seriously enough to invert the practice: own outcomes, keep metrics diagnostic and unowned. It will sign that assigning ownership changes the measure's behaviour. It will not sign that a register can be made gaming-proof by adding guardrails, since each guardrail is itself a target.

Figure 1. Most metric-governance failures are not failures of measurement but one of four empty slots, each failing in a recognisable way.

3. Mechanics: how cadence is actually derived

Competent practitioners set cadence by analogy — weekly, because the business review is weekly. Experts derive it from two independent constraints. The first is detection: at the proposed interval, can the metric distinguish the movement you care about from its own noise? The second is economics: does acting sooner buy more than meeting more often costs?

Take detection first. Approval rate is a proportion; on a weekday with 4,000 decisioned applications at a true rate near 0.62, the standard error of one day's rate is √(0.62 × 0.38 ÷ 4,000) = 0.77 percentage points, and comparing today with yesterday compounds two such errors to 1.09 points. The day-on-day wobble of ±1 point that Vindhya's operations channel debated every morning was therefore under one standard error: pure noise, discussed daily, occasionally acted on. Aggregate a week — 28,000 decisions — and the standard error falls to 0.29 points, making a one-point weekly move a 2.4-sigma signal. Reviewing this metric daily is not wasteful but harmful: it generates interventions in response to nothing, which is what Deming called tampering.

MetricVolume per intervalStd error of the levelSmallest move worth acting onImplied floor on cadence
Vindhya approval rate, daily4,0000.77 pt1.0 ptToo noisy — 0.9σ on a difference
Vindhya approval rate, weekly28,0000.29 pt1.0 ptWeekly works — 2.4σ
Shrenik burn-in fault rate, weekly6200.53 pt1.3 ptWeekly works — 2.4σ

The economic constraint yields a formula worth carrying in the head. Let C be the fully loaded cost of one review, λ the rate at which the regime genuinely shifts per day, and d the cost per day of operating in a shifted regime undetected. Reviewing every T days costs C/T per day, plus, since a shift arrives uniformly within the interval, an expected λ·d·T/2 in delay. Minimising the sum gives T* = √(2C / λd).

Vindhya's weekly funnel review costs about ₹1.1 lakh all-in. The funnel genuinely changes regime once in fifty working days, so λ ≈ 0.02, and a sustained one-point approval decline costs roughly ₹1 lakh a day in contribution margin at an average ticket of ₹78,000 and a 3.1% take. The optimum is √(2 × 1.1 ÷ 0.02) ≈ 10.5 days: fortnightly, not weekly. Run the same arithmetic on first-payment default for new co-lending cohorts. That review is cheaper — ₹0.4 lakh, three people and a standing query — and the regime shifts once in a hundred days, but a bad cohort still disbursing costs ₹14 lakh a day, giving T* = √(0.8 ÷ 0.14) ≈ 2.4 days. Same company, same calendar, two correct cadences differing fourfold.

Figure 2. Note the shape as much as the optimum: the green curve is nearly flat from six to twenty-five days, so roughly right is enough, while the red curve is steep only to the right of its optimum. Cadence errors are asymmetric.

That asymmetry is the second-order effect most practitioners miss: for low-stakes metrics the curve is flat and the weekly-versus-fortnightly argument is wasted, while for high-cost-of-delay metrics it is steep on one side only, so when uncertain, err fast. Three steps are usually left implicit. Write the decision rule in the imperative, naming the alternative action — "above 2.6% for two consecutive weeks, stop-ship and quarantine the batch" — not "informs quality strategy". Set the threshold in both directions, since unearned good news is the commonest source of quietly wrong attribution. And set the retirement trigger at creation, so a metric that has altered no decision in a stated number of cycles leaves the review automatically, without a defender having to lose an argument.

Retirement deserves its own arithmetic, because "nobody acts on it" is usually asserted rather than shown. Treat the review as a purchase of information. If a metric crosses its threshold with probability 3% in a week, and catching a crossing a week earlier is worth ₹22 lakh, the weekly look yields ₹0.66 lakh against ₹1.1 lakh of review cost — negative. Monthly, the crossing probability rises to about 12%, giving ₹2.64 lakh against the same ₹1.1 lakh. The metric was never worthless; its cadence was wrong, and the remedy was demotion, not deletion.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions can be stated as testable claims, and both protagonists fail at least one.

C1: the owner has at least one action, within their authority, that moves the metric inside one review interval. Ira fails this on blended approval and passes on a mix-adjusted version; Girish fails on the 30-day field fault rate at any cadence shorter than a quarter, and passes on a factory burn-in rate. C2: at the chosen cadence, the threshold movement is at least twice the metric's standard error. Vindhya's daily approval review fails and its weekly review passes; Shrenik's burn-in rate passes at 2.4σ. C3: expected cost of delay over one interval exceeds the cost of the review, which Vindhya's funnel fails weekly and passes fortnightly. C4: the metric is not mechanically determined by another owned metric, because two owners for the same information is one too many and the second defers. C5: no dominant gaming strategy is left uncovered by a paired guardrail.

Three situations make the discipline actively misleading. Before product–market fit, a register of owned metrics with thresholds ossifies a driver model that is still wrong; the right instrument is a weekly hypothesis review. During a deliberate regime break — a pricing change, a new regulation, a market entry — thresholds derived from the old regime fire spuriously or, worse, stay silent, and experts suspend the rule in writing rather than let it degrade. And during an incident the register's ownership map conflicts with incident command, so a company that cannot switch between the two spends its first thirty minutes deciding who is in charge.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The interesting failures live at seams. In a two-sided marketplace, the important metrics are ratios spanning both sides, and a ratio's owner can improve one by shrinking the denominator: approval rate rises if you stop originating marginal applicants. Mature marketplaces own numerator and denominator separately and review the ratio jointly: Nachiket owns routed volume and partner mix, Ira owns conversion within a fixed mix, and the blended rate is reported but owned by neither, flagged as an outcome rather than a lever.

In a regulated business the register acquires a second audience. Under the RBI's digital lending framework, certain disclosures and grievance-resolution timelines are not internal choices, and the cadence of the metrics evidencing them is set outside the company. Experts keep these in a separate compliance register with a named executive, never merged into the product review, because merging invites negotiation of a threshold that is not negotiable.

In hardware plus software, physics sets a floor on feedback, and Figure 3 shows why Girish's monthly metric could not have warned him. The mature response is not to review the lagging metric more often but to manufacture a leading one, give it a different owner and a faster cadence, and record the proxy's known biases in the register.

Figure 3. A lagging metric cannot be fixed by reviewing it more often. When feedback lag exceeds the decision interval, the register needs a second, faster metric with its own owner, marked as a proxy.

In multi-product companies the seam is definitional rather than temporal. Yatharth Retail Cloud, which sells point-of-sale, inventory, loyalty and analytics modules to retail chains from Gurugram, reported 41,200 weekly active merchants to its board through 2025. Each product team owned its activation metric honestly, but a merchant using three modules was counted three times at the top: the de-duplicated figure was 33,700. The gap was not fraud but the absence of a definition owner above the product line. Yatharth's fix was to separate definition ownership from decision ownership — one person in data governance may change what "active merchant" means, publishes a dated changelog, and cannot be overruled inside a review.

In AI-native products the seam is the model release. At Vachan Health AI, a Hyderabad company whose scribe drafts clinical notes for outpatient consultations, the headline metric is the share of notes accepted without edit. Model versions ship every three weeks and move it by three to six points — larger than any week-to-week operational variation — so the trend line is uninterpretable unless cut by version. Good AI teams add a version column to the register, compare only within-version cohorts, and require the owner to control or co-sign the release calendar. Such companies say they govern AI metrics like any other; what they actually do is treat model version as a confound of the same class as a pricing change.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Instrumented, reviewed, and owned are three different states

Competent teams conflate retiring a metric with deleting it; the expert keeps almost everything instrumented and prunes only the review. The tell is a post-mortem in which nobody can reconstruct events because a dashboard was "cleaned up" two quarters ago. The obvious reading — that dashboard bloat is the disease — is wrong: a metric's cost is the attention it consumes in a room, not the storage it occupies.

The binding constraint on cadence is whichever is slower: acting or knowing

Practitioners set cadence to decision latency alone. Experts take the maximum of decision and detection latency, and notice the two can be attacked separately: Vindhya's problem was detection-bound and solved by aggregation, Shrenik's was feedback-bound and solved by a new measurement point. The tell is a team reviewing a metric more often than its confidence interval narrows, and explaining each week's movement anyway.

Ownership of a single number is an invitation; ownership of a pair is a contract

Grove's paired indicators are routinely quoted and rarely implemented, because the guardrail usually belongs to another function on another cadence — precisely the gap a rational owner exploits with no intent to cheat. The tell is a metric improving smartly while a neighbouring number degrades slowly in a deck nobody in this meeting reads.

The "decision it informs" must name an alternative action

If the sentence contains the words informs, tracks, monitors or guides, there is no decision. The expert's test is to make the owner complete: "if this crosses X, we stop doing A and start doing B." Teams find this excruciating, which is the point — the difficulty is evidence that the metric's purpose was never articulated, not that the exercise is pedantic.

Mix effects make an honest owner look dishonest

Vindhya's blended approval rate fell 4.5 points while every partner's own rate rose. The expert's instinct on seeing any aggregate ratio move is to ask for the decomposition before the explanation, and to own the mix-adjusted number separately from the mix. The tell is an aggregate moving while every segment moves the other way, and a room accepting the story because a senior person has begun explaining it. Cadence should be state-dependent for the same reason: festival peaks, renewals and regulatory windows change the mix, and escalation belongs in the register rather than depending on who happens to be worried.

Ownership attaches to a role in a register, never to a person in a slide

Reorganisations orphan metrics silently, because the leaving manager's numbers appear on nobody's transition checklist. Experts run an orphan audit within two weeks of any structural change: every metric read aloud, every name confirmed. The tell is an owner who says they thought someone else had picked it up.

The review itself is a metric

Decision yield — decisions altered per review — is the only honest measure of whether a cadence earns its cost. Experts track it, publish it, and use it rather than intuition when demoting metrics. The tell is a review that has become a status report: long, well-attended, calm, and followed by no changed plans.

Definition drift is more dangerous than value drift

A number that moves gets attention; a number whose meaning moves does not. A tracking-plan change, a silent filter edit, a time-zone correction each shifts the series without alarm. The expert requires definition changes to be dated, announced, and either backfilled or explicitly not, and treats an unannounced change as an incident.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

The real differences across product types concern statistical power, feedback lag and who holds the lever. In consumer products volume is high and cadence is limited by decision latency rather than detection, so a daily metric is genuinely readable and the problem is restraint. In B2B and enterprise the reverse holds: with 180 accounts no proportion is readable weekly, so the review becomes account-level and qualitative, ownership sits jointly with customer success, and cadence anchors to renewal dates. Practitioners who import consumer habits here review numbers that cannot move, then conclude the metrics are wrong when the cadence is.

In platforms and marketplaces ratio metrics resist single ownership, and the honest structure splits numerator from denominator. In hardware, lag dominates and the register must reach into supply chain and quality, where product has influence and no authority. In AI products three things are genuinely different: model version is a first-class confound; unit cost of inference is a product metric with a real owner rather than an engineering footnote — Vachan's cost per note rose from ₹2.40 to ₹4.10 with one release, ₹4.42 lakh a month at 260,000 notes; and evaluation metrics live on a release cadence while product metrics live on a business cadence, so the two must be reconciled explicitly rather than merged.

Where the difference is claimed and is not real: the four-slot contract itself applies identically to a consumer app and a turbine monitoring system. Only the parameters change.

Stage changes the practice more than product type does. Before product–market fit a register is ceremony. Between roughly fifty and three hundred people it becomes load-bearing, because no one person can hold the tree and the review is the only place accountability is visible. Past a thousand people the problem inverts: the scarce resource is definitional coherence, which is why companies at that scale invest in semantic layers and metric stores, and why the definition owner — a role that looked like bureaucracy at Series B — becomes the most consequential seat in the room. For listed companies, externally reported metrics acquire a disclosure cadence set by SEBI filing requirements, and internal thresholds cannot be quietly re-derived in ways that change a published series.

8. Three worked examples

Vindhya, and the mix that hid in plain sight. Zoya's decomposition took three hours and settled the August argument. Partner A, the most permissive underwriter, had cut its share of routed volume after tightening its own policy; the most conservative partner absorbed it.

Holding mix at June weights, approval had risen 1.5 points while the headline fell 4.5; the six-point gap was mix, and mix was Nachiket's lever, not Ira's. Two years of a metric whose owner could not move it had produced two years of product investment aimed at the wrong constraint.

Shrenik, and the metric that was manufactured. Girish stopped arguing for a faster field metric and built one at the factory: a 72-hour powered burn-in fault rate on every unit, owned by Ravindra Salunke in Pune, reviewed weekly, with a pre-committed rule. Baseline was 1.8% on about 620 units a week, standard error 0.53 points. In the week of 22 June the rate was 3.1% — 2.4 standard errors — and 2.9% the week after; two consecutive weeks above 2.6% would now trigger automatic batch quarantine. Run retrospectively, the rule would have stopped shipment in the first week of July, five weeks before Girish stood on the shop floor, saving roughly ₹2.1 crore of the ₹3.03 crore field-replacement bill. The lagging field metric was demoted, not retired: monthly, under Lalitha, with recall or no recall as its decision — which genuinely belongs on a monthly clock.

Tamasha Play, where the discipline was applied and failed. Tamasha is a Bengaluru live-commerce video app. In January 2026 its growth lead, Sarika Dhawan, was given clean single-threaded ownership of watch minutes per daily active user, a target of +15% by June, and a weekly cadence: textbook practice. She shipped autoplay chaining and a 9 p.m. push; the metric went from 24.6 to 29.3 minutes, up 19.1%. Every guardrail that mattered sat outside her register. Order return rate, owned by category operations and reviewed monthly, rose from 18.2% to 26.7%, an extra ₹2.9 crore a quarter in refunds and reverse logistics; notification opt-out went from 6% to 19%; ninety-day retention of the January cohort fell from 31.4% to 24.8%. None of this was misconduct — the system was designed to produce exactly this. Recovery took two quarters and about ₹6.1 crore, and watch minutes was re-specified as a pair reviewed jointly with return rate, with an automatic halt on the push above 9% opt-out. The instructive part is what did not recover: opt-out returned only to 12% after eight months, because users who disable notifications rarely re-enable them. Some guardrails are springs and some are ratchets, and a ratchet deserves a tighter threshold and faster cadence than its cost of delay alone would justify.

Each failure is caught cheaply by a question about authority or timing, and expensively by a number. The questions cost minutes; by the time the number tells you, the cost has been incurred. Two more belong on the list: committee ownership, caught by asking who can change the plan alone today, and ritual drift, caught by asking what changed because of last month's reviews.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should an owner be accountable for a metric they cannot control? The controllability camp argues that holding Ira accountable for blended approval caused two years of misdirected work and, generally, drives good managers out of roles where variance is exogenous; its evidence is the management-accounting literature on responsibility-centre design and the behaviour of owners who explain rather than act. The informativeness camp, following Holmström, argues that filtering to controllable signals discards information: a noisy metric still says something about effort, and an owner insulated from outcomes optimises inputs. It would be wrong if the cost of gaming and attrition under noisy accountability exceeded the information gained — an empirical question no company runs the experiment to settle.

One owner or two on interface metrics? The single-threaded camp's evidence is organisational: shared ownership degrades into deferral, silently. The joint-ownership camp points to two-sided ratios where any single owner has a dominant strategy harmful to the business, and argues for a jointly owned pair with a shared threshold rather than a false assignment. It would be wrong if joint pairs produced the same deferral with more meetings — precisely what the first camp claims happens.

Do rituals still earn their cost against alerting? The automation camp observes that a pre-committed rule can fire continuously at zero marginal cost, and that a weekly meeting is a batch process defended by habit. The ritual camp replies that reviews produce what alerts cannot — shared context, cross-functional trades, the social fact of someone standing up and answering — and that alert-only regimes reliably produce fatigue and, within a year, muted channels. It would be wrong if a company could show sustained low alert-acknowledgement latency over years without a standing forum.

Should metrics be targets at all? The anti-target camp — Goodhart applied seriously, and the Beyond Budgeting tradition — holds that a measure becomes unreliable the moment it becomes a target, so metrics should stay diagnostic while accountability attaches to outcomes. Its evidence is every gamed target in the record, Tamasha's included. The mainstream reply is that unowned metrics are simply ignored, and that guardrail pairs contain gaming well enough in practice. It would be wrong if guardrails proved gameable at the same rate as the metrics they protect.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this can recite the four slots. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask "what would you do differently?" before "what is the number?", and refuse ownership in public when the answer is nothing. They write thresholds and retirement triggers at creation, when writing them is cheap and nobody is defending anything. They treat cadence as a derived quantity, carry the square roots in their head, and are unembarrassed to move a flagship metric to fortnightly. And they attend to seams by reflex: the orphan audit after a reorganisation, the decomposition before the explanation, and, on seeing a metric improve sharply, the question of what its pair did.

12. What Ira and Girish decided

Ira split the metric rather than defending it. Mix-adjusted approval, held at fixed partner mix, became hers on a fortnightly cadence, deciding whether to fund or defer funnel and document-capture work. Partner mix and routed volume became Nachiket's weekly, deciding routing and commercial renegotiation. Blended approval stayed on the board pack, labelled an outcome with no owner and no threshold — an entry she had to defend twice. First-payment default moved to every second day with an automatic pause rule, and eleven of thirty-four tiles left the review while staying fully instrumented.

Girish refused an assignment instead of accepting one. He declined weekly ownership of the 30-day field fault rate on the explicit ground that no action of his changed it inside a month, and committed instead to the burn-in rate under Ravindra, with the two-week stop-ship rule written before the next batch ran. Shrenik's register gained a column nobody had thought to add: expected feedback lag, in weeks, for every metric in the review.

  1. Vindhya's blended approval rate now appears on the board pack with no owner and no threshold. Is an explicitly unowned metric a useful category, or an admission that nobody is responsible for the company's most-quoted number?
  2. Sarika Dhawan did everything the textbook asked: a single owner, a clear target, a weekly cadence. Was Tamasha's failure one of the discipline, or of the people who left the guardrail outside her register — and does the distinction change what you would do?
  3. Shrenik's burn-in rate is a proxy whose relationship to field failure is unmeasured. When is a fast proxy of unknown bias better than a slow measure of the thing you actually care about, and how would you know when it stops being so?

13. Going deeper

Metric trees and driver models is the prerequisite: ownership can be assigned node by node only if the decomposition is causally honest, and a bad tree assigns real accountability for imaginary levers. Cross-functional rituals is where cadence lives — a cadence not on a calendar with an agenda and a decision log is an intention, not a rhythm. What makes a good metric is the upstream filter: sensitivity, timeliness and resistance to gaming decide whether a metric can bear an owner at all. Vanity versus actionable metrics applies that filter to retirement, and gives you language for removing a number someone likes. The GAME framework moves from goal to action to metric, which is what produces the "decision it informs" sentence rather than improvising it. Acquisition, retention and monetisation actions tells you which function holds which lever, and so who may legitimately own each node. Direct versus proxy, magnitude versus ratio is the technical core behind Shrenik's proxy and Vindhya's denominator problem. And the north star metric sits at the top of the tree, where ownership is most assumed and least examined: the one number whose owner is usually the whole company, which is to say nobody.
